newsitem.title: USA: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- Next stop for bonds: 6.25 pct.
newsitem.headline: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- Next stop for bonds: 6.25 pct.

text.p: The yield on the U.S. Treasury 30-year bond is poised to drop to the key 6.25 percent level, unthinkable just a few months ago, but a further decline may prove difficult, market players said.
The bond on Thursday morning came the closest it has been to that critical level since mid-February 1996, falling as low as 6.29 percent from 6.32 percent on Wednesday.

"We could get there tomorrow (Friday), right after employment," said Paul Roberti, head bond salesman at Yamaichi International (America) Inc, referring to the release of the widely watched employment report for July. "It should be no bigger trouble getting to than other levels."
Ahead of next week's quarterly refunding, the when-issued 30-year bond yield fell as low as 6.2549 percent early Thursday.

Just a few months ago, when bonds were above 7 percent, a 6.25 percent long bond was unthinkable. Even 6.50 percent or 6.75 percent was hardly credible, as many predicted the Fed would raise rates again. Each time resistance was shattered, players were quick to say that breaking through the next level would be difficult.

But a much improved U.S. budget picture and scant danger of a pickup in inflation, along with flows from mortgages and friendly statements from Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan fueled a huge rally.
Still, market participants said that once the bond gets there, it may have difficulty breaching below the 6-1/4 percent level.

For starters, the next resistance level is at 6.245 percent (corresponding to about 117-1/2 on the bond contract), making 6-1/4 percent not only a psychological level but a technical one as well. And that would only put the spread between the bond and federal funds target rate -- currently 5.50 percent and going nowhere -- at a very tight 75 basis points.
One 30-year trader at a primary dealership said that once the bond yield reaches 6-1/4 percent, he will "feel good" about shorting the issue -- a sentiment echoed by others.
"You will find sellers there," added Brett Benza, senior trader at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. "We have already identified sellers" when the bond falls to 6.25 percent.

The pause may only be temporary. At this time, some players see no reason for the bond not to keep surging ahead, and adding to the gains in July that took the 30-year from 6.78 percent on July 1 to its current level.

Inflation remains comfortably low, despite a healthy economy and strong labor market. Along with a firm dollar and a nearly balanced federal budget deficit cutting the amount of debt sold by the government, many players do not see why the bond can't fall to 6.0 percent, or even 5.80 percent.
"It's new world," said one trader. "You have to kind of adjust your standards because things have changed. Given where stock prices are, I don't think 6 percent is pricey at all."
That's because historic relationships have seemingly changed. "It seems the risk premium is declining," said Tom Macirowski, fixed income strategist at Goldman Sachs & Co.

He noted that it is unclear where "fair value" on the bond lies. In the 1960s, a similar time when inflation was low with a favorable fiscal environment, the average spread between the overnight bank lending rate and the 10-year note (the longest issue at the time) was about 60 basis points.
Therefore, Macirowski said, a 75 basis point spread between fed funds and the long bond is fair, but even a 50 basis point spread may be considered fair value as well.
"It will not be an orderly march to 6 percent," said a bond trader. "To get there, you will have to see slowing in the economy."
